items.name: THE FLOPPY DISK
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a 3.5-inch floppy disk
items.epitaph: Once found on every desk; now preserved inside the Save icon.
items.why: Smaller, faster, and vastly larger storage made its tiny capacity and fragile magnetic media impractical.
items.afterlife: Specialist manufacturers, old machinery, collectors, and one remarkably durable icon keep it alive.
items.note: 2011 marks the end of Sony's 3.5-inch floppy production, not the disappearance of every floppy disk.

items.name: CONCORDE
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of Concorde in flight
items.epitaph: The future crossed the Atlantic faster than sound, then returned to subsonic speed.
items.why: High operating costs, limited routes, falling demand, and the aftermath of the 2000 crash ended commercial service.
items.afterlife: All surviving aircraft are preserved; none remains airworthy for passenger service.
items.note: The lifespan runs from first flight to final commercial service.

items.name: GOOGLE READER
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of an RSS feed reader
items.epitaph: It organized the open web before algorithms decided what we should read.
items.why: Google retired the service as usage declined while the company narrowed its product focus.
items.afterlife: RSS survived in independent readers, podcasts, and a smaller but stubbornly open ecosystem.

items.name: THE iPOD
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a click-wheel music player
items.epitaph: A thousand songs left the pocket when the pocket became a phone.
items.why: Music playback became one function of the iPhone and other connected devices instead of a separate product.
items.afterlife: Used iPods, repair communities, and the click wheel preserve a distraction-free way to listen.
items.note: Apple ended the product line after selling remaining iPod touch stock.

items.name: ADOBE FLASH PLAYER
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a browser plug-in being removed
items.epitaph: For a while, the web moved, played, and wasted lunch breaks inside one browser plug-in.
items.why: Open web standards matured while security, performance, and mobile compatibility made the plug-in model untenable.
items.afterlife: Preservation projects and emulators keep thousands of Flash games and animations accessible.

items.name: THE SPACE SHUTTLE
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a Space Shuttle orbiter over Earth
items.epitaph: It made orbit look almost routine. It never truly was.
items.why: NASA completed the program after 30 years, shifting resources toward new spacecraft and exploration goals.
items.afterlife: The surviving orbiters are museum exhibits, while their engineering legacy continues across human spaceflight.
items.note: The final mission, STS-135, ended on 21 July 2011.

items.name: PAN AM
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a 1970s jumbo jet at an airport
items.epitaph: Its blue globe once meant that the wider world was finally within reach.
items.why: Deregulation, rising costs, debt, and the loss of key assets left the pioneering airline unable to continue.
items.afterlife: Its routes, terminals, branding, and jet-age mythology remain embedded in commercial aviation history.
items.note: Pan American World Airways ceased operations in December 1991.

items.name: THE PASSENGER PIGEON
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history illustration of a passenger pigeon
items.epitaph: Billions filled the sky. Within a human lifetime, not one remained.
items.why: Industrial-scale hunting and destruction of its forest habitat drove a once-abundant species to extinction.
items.afterlife: Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, is preserved at the Smithsonian.
items.source_name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
items.note: Martha died at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914.

items.name: THE GREAT AUK
items.image_alt: Monochrome natural-history illustration of a great auk
items.epitaph: A flightless bird of the North Atlantic, collected until there was nothing left to collect.
items.why: Centuries of hunting for food, feathers, oil, and specimens eliminated the species from its nesting islands.
items.afterlife: Skins, skeletons, eggs, and museum records are all that remain.
items.note: The last widely accepted breeding pair was killed in Iceland in 1844.

items.name: BLOCKBUSTER VIDEO STORES
items.image_alt: Monochrome illustration of a 1990s video-rental store
items.epitaph: Friday-night choice once required fluorescent light, plastic cases, and a little negotiation.
items.why: Streaming and mail-order rentals replaced the cost and inconvenience of maintaining thousands of physical stores.
items.afterlife: One independently owned Blockbuster store still trades in Bend, Oregon.
items.note: The brand is not literally extinct; the Bend store remains open.
